entry.title: Why Pass/Fail CI Pipelines Break Down—and How Risk‑Based Quality Gates Fix It
entry.summary:
Most CI/CD pipelines still make release decisions using a binary model: ✅ Tests passed → deploy That model works well for small systems. The Problem with Pass/Fail Gates All failures are equal In enterprise environments, those assumptions stop being true. Severity of failures As a result, teams often: Override automated blocks When automation is frequently bypassed, it stops being a safety mechanism and becomes background noise. Release Readiness Is a Decision Problem “Did tests fail?” They ask: *“Where is the risk, how severe is it, and does this warrant human review?”
To reflect that reality, release decisions need at least three outcomes, not two: ✅ GO — acceptable risk The middle state matters. It’s where judgment, accountability, and governance live. A Risk‑Based Quality Gate Model Ingests test results as pipeline artifacts Crucially, it also explains that decision. Over‑blocking on low‑impact failures Example: Explainable High‑Risk Release Decision The pipeline produces: This output makes three things explicit: Why the release is blocked The goal isn’t to replace human judgment—but to support it with transparent evidence. Why This Works Better Than Binary Gates Trust in automation Governance and auditability Signal‑to‑noise ratio Alignment with real decision‑making Reference Implementation https://github.com/gaya3bollineni/risk-based-quality-gate/releases/tag/v1.0.0 No CI plugins It is designed to be run inside a CI/CD pipeline as a decision‑support step, not as an opaque enforcement mechanism. Final Thought If your pipeline frequently asks humans to override its decisions, the automation isn’t failing—the decision model is. Risk‑based quality gates acknowledge uncertainty, surface context, and formalize the handoff between automation and human accountability. That’s not adding complexity. It’s matching reality.

entry.summary: Compare x402 and Tempo’s MPP for HTTP 402-based API payments, including protocol design, payment methods, charge vs session billing, settlement and receipts, and when to use each with Quicknode’s x402 SDKs or its MPP endpoint for machine-to-machine and RPC workflows.
